lead: A flame photometer measures sodium, potassium, lithium, calcium or barium by the light their atoms emit in a hot flame. A diluted sample is sprayed into the flame. Atoms absorb heat, become excited, and fall back emitting light at fixed wavelengths. A filter selects one wavelength and a photodetector measures the brightness. The method exists because these elements are hard to measure by simple colour reactions and are common in clinical samples: sodium and potassium in serum and urine, and lithium in patients on lithium therapy. It is fast, cheap and needs only a small sample.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for the source–monochromator–detector–readout chain and for calibration curves.

blocks.text: An alkali metal atom in a hot flame takes in thermal energy and reaches an excited state. It stays there for a very short time, of the order of 10 nanoseconds, and then falls back. On falling back it emits light at wavelengths fixed by its electron levels. The wavelength is a fingerprint of the element. Sodium gives a strong yellow line at 589 nm, potassium a line at 766 nm, and lithium a line at 671 nm. The symbol nm means nanometre, 10⁻⁹ m. The brightness of the emitted line depends on how many atoms of that element are in the flame. More atoms give more light. This is emission, not absorption: the instrument does not shine its own light through the sample. Only elements that are easily excited in a flame work well: sodium, potassium, lithium, calcium and barium. Clinical use is mostly sodium and potassium in serum and urine, and lithium for patients on lithium therapy.

The sample must first be diluted because serum contains about 140 mmol/L sodium and 4 mmol/L potassium, which is too high for the linear range. A dilution of 1:50 to 1:200 is common, made in a diluent that already holds a fixed amount of lithium (the internal standard, below). A nebulizer turns the diluted sample into a fine spray, and only the finest droplets reach the flame.

The flame is air with LPG (propane or butane), at about 1900 °C, or air with acetylene, at about 2200–2300 °C. The cooler LPG flame is enough to excite sodium, potassium and lithium, and it excites few other elements, which keeps interference low. Water evaporates, salts break into atoms, and a small fraction of the atoms become excited.

The light from the flame passes a lens and an interference filter (or a monochromator) that selects one line: 589 nm for sodium, 766 nm for potassium, or 671 nm for lithium. Each line has its own filter and photodetector, so the channels are read together. The potassium line at 766 nm lies at the red edge of the visible band, where many detectors chosen for the yellow sodium line are weak, so that channel needs a red-sensitive detector such as a silicon photodiode. An amplifier raises each signal and the readout displays a number.

blocks.where: R is the readout in arbitrary units; C<sub>d</sub> is the diluted concentration in mmol/L; k is a constant found by calibration.

blocks.text: The chain follows the same source–monochromator–detector–readout idea as 3.1, but the source is the flame itself and no lamp shines through the sample.
Calibration uses a blank (diluent alone) and at least one standard of known concentration, run under the same flame. For a one-point calibration:

blocks.where: C<sub>serum</sub> is the original serum concentration in mmol/L; C<sub>std</sub> is the standard concentration in mmol/L, made up at the diluted strength; R<sub>sample</sub> and R<sub>std</sub> are the readouts for sample and standard in the same units; D is the dilution factor.

blocks.text: For 1:50 dilution D = 50; for 1:100, D = 100. With an internal standard, the instrument reads ratios instead of single lines: sodium-to-lithium on the sodium channel and potassium-to-lithium on the potassium channel. Lithium is used because healthy serum has almost none of it and its line at 671 nm is clear of the other two. Flame flicker, viscosity differences and small changes in spray rate change all the lines by the same fraction, so each ratio cancels much of the error. The ratio then takes the place of R in the formula. When lithium itself is to be measured, for a patient on lithium therapy, the lithium internal standard cannot be used, and lithium is read directly against lithium standards or with another element as the internal standard.

Common errors are other ions, flame drift, a blocked capillary and too high a concentration. At high concentration, atoms near the cool edge of the flame absorb light from excited atoms, so the curve bends downward; this is self-absorption. A blocked capillary gives a low, noisy signal. An atomic absorption spectrophotometer (AAS) measures light absorbed from a separate hollow-cathode lamp, while a flame photometer measures emitted light. Both need calibration and both can measure sodium and potassium, but the measurement principles are opposite.

figure.caption: A flame photometer with a lithium internal standard: the diluted serum is sprayed into an air–LPG flame, and filters split the emitted light into the sodium, potassium and lithium lines. The potassium line at 766 nm needs a red-sensitive detector. In worked example 2 the K/Li ratio of 0.42 against 0.50 for a 0.10 mmol/L standard gives 4.2 mmol/L.

examples.question: A serum sample is diluted 1:50 and run in a flame photometer. The readout is 40 units. A 2.0 mmol/L sodium standard gives 32 units under the same flame. Find the sodium concentration in the diluted sample and in the original serum, and say whether the value is normal.
steps: A 1:50 dilution means one part serum is made up to 50 parts with diluent, so the dilution factor is D = 50.
For the same flame, readout is proportional to diluted concentration: R<sub>sample</sub> / R<sub>std</sub> = C<sub>d</sub> / C<sub>std</sub>.
The original serum is 50 times more concentrated: C<sub>serum</sub> = C<sub>d</sub> × D = 2.5 mmol/L × 50 = 125 mmol/L.
The serum sodium reference range is about 135–145 mmol/L, so 125 mmol/L is low (hyponatraemia). A low result is repeated with a fresh dilution before it is reported.
examples.answer: The diluted sample contains 2.5 mmol/L sodium, so the original serum contains 125 mmol/L, which is below the normal range.

examples.question: Serum is diluted 1:50 in a diluent that contains lithium. On the potassium channel the potassium-to-lithium ratio is 0.42. A 0.10 mmol/L potassium standard made in the same diluent gives a ratio of 0.50. (a) Find the serum potassium. (b) The spray rate then falls by 10 %. What happens to the potassium signal and to the ratio?
steps: The ratio takes the place of R in the one-point formula: C<sub>d</sub> = C<sub>std</sub> × (ratio<sub>sample</sub> / ratio<sub>std</sub>).
C<sub>d</sub> = 0.10 mmol/L × (0.42 / 0.50) = 0.10 × 0.84 = 0.084 mmol/L in the diluted sample.
C<sub>serum</sub> = 0.084 mmol/L × 50 = 4.2 mmol/L. The reference range is about 3.5–5.0 mmol/L, so this is normal.
If the spray rate falls by 10 %, fewer atoms of both elements reach the flame, so the potassium signal and the lithium signal both fall to 0.90 of their old values.
The ratio is (0.90 × K signal) / (0.90 × Li signal) = the same 0.42, so the result stays 4.2 mmol/L. Without the internal standard the reading would fall by 10 %, to about 3.8 mmol/L.
examples.answer: (a) Serum potassium = 4.2 mmol/L. (b) Both signals fall by 10 %, the ratio stays 0.42 and the result stays 4.2 mmol/L; a single-line reading would have dropped to about 3.8 mmol/L.

traps: Forgetting the dilution factor: 2.5 mmol/L is the diluted concentration; the serum value is 125 mmol/L in the worked example.
Calling the measurement absorption, or applying the Beer–Lambert law directly to the emitted flame light. A flame photometer measures emission.
Using the wrong filter: sodium is read at 589 nm, potassium at 766 nm, and lithium at 671 nm.
Calibrating only at high concentration, where self-absorption bends the curve downward and makes the sample look lower than it is.
Ignoring the internal standard and flame drift, then reporting a false potassium result; the potassium channel also reads a ratio to lithium.

quiz.q: Which elements are commonly measured by flame photometry in clinical samples?
quiz.a: Sodium and potassium in serum and urine; lithium for therapy monitoring. Calcium and barium are possible but less common clinically.

quiz.q: Why is the flame photometer called an emission instrument, not an absorption instrument?
quiz.a: It measures light emitted by excited atoms in the flame. It does not measure light absorbed from a separate lamp; that is AAS.

quiz.q: Serum is diluted 1:100 and gives a reading of 28. A 1.5 mmol/L sodium standard gives 30. Find the diluted and serum sodium concentrations.
quiz.a: C<sub>d</sub> = 1.5 × 28/30 = 1.4 mmol/L. C<sub>serum</sub> = 1.4 × 100 = 140 mmol/L, inside the normal range of about 135–145 mmol/L.

quiz.q: Why does the calibration curve bend downward at very high sodium concentration?
quiz.a: Self-absorption: cooler atoms absorb light emitted by excited atoms. The readout rises less than proportional, so a high sample can be underestimated if not diluted.

quiz.q: What does an internal lithium standard cancel in a flame photometer?
quiz.a: It cancels flame flicker, viscosity and spray-rate changes, because these change the sodium, potassium and lithium lines by the same fraction; the instrument reads the sodium-to-lithium and potassium-to-lithium ratios.

quiz.q: A flame photometer gives low, noisy potassium readings. List two likely causes and one check for each.
quiz.a: Blocked capillary: check spray and cleaning. Flame drift or fuel/air change: run the standard again. Also check for the wrong filter or contaminated glassware.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern laboratories often measure sodium and potassium with ion-selective electrodes, while flame photometry remains a reference and teaching method. Lithium therapy monitoring still uses flame emission or an ion-selective electrode. Newer work couples microfluidics and low-cost photodiodes to flame emission. Search terms: flame emission spectroscopy, internal standard, self-absorption, ion-selective electrode sodium potassium.
